paragraphs: The Karamazovs’ house stood a good way from the center of the town, but it wasn’t quite on the outskirts either. It was a pleasant-looking old house of two stories, painted gray, with a red iron roof. It was roomy and snug, and it could still last many years. It was full of unexpected little cupboards, closets and staircases. There were rats in it, but Fyodor Pavlovitch didn’t altogether mind them. “You don’t feel so lonely when you’re left by yourself in the evening,” he used to say. He had a habit of sending the servants off to the lodge for the night and locking himself in alone. The lodge was a roomy, solid building in the yard. Fyodor Pavlovitch had the cooking done there, although the house had a kitchen of its own. He disliked the smell of cooking, so winter and summer alike the dishes were carried across the courtyard. The house had been built for a large family, with room for five times as many people, servants included. But at the time of our story nobody lived in the house except Fyodor Pavlovitch and his son Ivan. And in the lodge there were only three servants: old Grigory, his old wife Marfa, and a young man called Smerdyakov. I must say a few words about these three. Of old Grigory I have said something already. He was firm and determined. Once he had been brought, by whatever reasons (and they were often very illogical ones), to believe that something was unalterably right, he went at it blindly and stubbornly. He was honest and incorruptible. His wife, Marfa Ignatyevna, had obeyed her husband’s will without question all her life, yet she had pestered him terribly after the emancipation of the serfs. She was set on leaving Fyodor Pavlovitch and opening a little shop in Moscow with their small savings. But Grigory decided then, once and for all, that “the woman is talking nonsense, for every woman is dishonest,” and that they must not leave their old master, whatever he might be, for “that was their duty now.”
“Do you understand what duty is?” he asked Marfa Ignatyevna.
“I understand what duty means, Grigory Vassilyevitch, but why it’s our duty to stay here I’ll never understand,” Marfa answered firmly.
“Well, then, don’t understand. But that’s how it’s going to be. And hold your tongue.”

And so it was. They didn’t leave, and Fyodor Pavlovitch promised them a small wage and paid it regularly. Grigory knew, too, that he had an undeniable influence over his master. It was true, and he was aware of it. Fyodor Pavlovitch was a stubborn and cunning buffoon. His will was strong enough “in some of the affairs of life,” as he put it, yet he found himself, to his own surprise, extremely weak in facing certain other emergencies. He knew his weaknesses and was afraid of them. There are situations in which a man has to keep a sharp lookout. That’s not easy without a trustworthy person, and Grigory was a most trustworthy man. Many times in his life Fyodor Pavlovitch had narrowly escaped a good thrashing thanks to Grigory’s intervention, and each time the old servant gave him a sound lecture. But it wasn’t only thrashings that Fyodor Pavlovitch feared. There were graver occasions, very subtle and complicated ones, when Fyodor Pavlovitch couldn’t have explained the extraordinary craving for someone faithful and devoted that sometimes came over him, unaccountably, all in a moment. It was almost a sickness. Corrupt and often cruel in his lust, like some poisonous insect, Fyodor Pavlovitch was sometimes overcome, in his drunken moments, by a superstitious terror and a moral convulsion that showed itself almost physically. “My soul’s simply quaking in my throat at those times,” he used to say. At such moments he liked to feel that a strong, faithful man was close at hand, in the lodge if not in the room. He wanted someone virtuous and unlike himself, who had seen all his debauchery and knew all his secrets, but who was ready, out of devotion, to overlook all that. This man was not to oppose him, and above all not to reproach him or threaten him with anything, in this world or the next. In case of need he was to defend him—from whom? From somebody unknown, but terrible and dangerous. What he needed was to feel that there was _another_ man, an old and tried friend, whom he could call in his sick moments just to look at his face, or perhaps to exchange a few quite irrelevant words. If the old servant wasn’t angry, he felt comforted, and if he was angry, he felt more dejected. It even happened (though very rarely) that Fyodor Pavlovitch went to the lodge at night to wake Grigory and bring him over for a moment. When the old man came, Fyodor Pavlovitch would start talking about the most trivial matters and soon let him go again, sometimes even with a joke. And after Grigory had gone, Fyodor Pavlovitch would get into bed with a curse and sleep the sleep of the just. Something of the same sort had happened to Fyodor Pavlovitch when Alyosha arrived. Alyosha “pierced his heart” by “living with him, seeing everything and blaming nothing.” What’s more, Alyosha brought with him something his father had never known before: a complete absence of contempt for him, an unfailing kindness, and a perfectly natural, unaffected devotion to an old man who deserved it so little. All this was a complete surprise to the old profligate, who had dropped all family ties. It was a new and astonishing experience for a man who until then had loved nothing but “evil.” When Alyosha had left him, he admitted to himself that he had learned something he hadn’t been willing to learn before.

I have already mentioned that Grigory had detested Adelaïda Ivanovna, the first wife of Fyodor Pavlovitch and the mother of Dmitri. On the other hand, he had protected Sofya Ivanovna, the poor “crazy woman,” against his master and against anyone who happened to speak ill or lightly of her. His sympathy for the unhappy wife had become something sacred to him. Even now, twenty years later, he couldn’t bear a slighting remark about her from anyone, and he would check the offender at once. On the outside, Grigory was cold, dignified and silent. He spoke weighing his words, and never frivolously. You couldn’t tell at first sight whether he loved his meek, obedient wife, but he really did love her, and she knew it.

Marfa Ignatyevna was by no means a fool. She was probably cleverer than her husband, or at least more prudent than he in worldly affairs, and yet she had given in to him in everything, without question or complaint, ever since their marriage, and she respected him for his spiritual superiority. It was remarkable how little they spoke to each other in the course of their lives, and then only about the most necessary daily matters. The grave and dignified Grigory thought over all his cares and duties alone, so that Marfa Ignatyevna had long been used to knowing that he didn’t need her advice. She felt that her husband respected her silence and took it as a sign of good sense. He had beaten her only once, and then only lightly. It happened in the year after Fyodor Pavlovitch’s marriage to Adelaïda Ivanovna. The village girls and women—serfs at that time—were called together in front of the house to sing and dance. They were starting “In the Green Meadows” when Marfa, then a young woman, skipped forward and danced “the Russian Dance.” She didn’t dance it in the village style, but as she had danced it when she was a servant in the rich Miüsov family, in their private theater, where the actors were taught to dance by a dancing master from Moscow. Grigory saw how his wife danced, and an hour later, at home in their cottage, he gave her a lesson, pulling her hair a little. But that was the end of it: the beating was never repeated, and Marfa Ignatyevna gave up dancing.

God had not blessed them with children. One child was born, but it died. Grigory was fond of children and wasn’t ashamed to show it. When Adelaïda Ivanovna ran away, Grigory took Dmitri, who was then three years old, combed his hair and washed him in a tub with his own hands, and looked after him for almost a year. Afterwards he looked after Ivan and Alyosha, for which the general’s widow rewarded him with a slap in the face; but I have already told all that. The only happiness his own child had brought him was in looking forward to its birth. When it was born, he was overwhelmed with grief and horror. The baby had six fingers. Grigory was so crushed by this that he stayed silent until the day of the christening, and kept away in the garden. It was spring, and he spent three days digging the kitchen garden. The third day was the one fixed for christening the baby. In the meantime Grigory had reached a conclusion. He went into the cottage, where the clergy had gathered and the visitors had arrived, including Fyodor Pavlovitch, who was to be godfather. There he suddenly announced that the baby “ought not to be christened at all.” He said this quietly and briefly, forcing out the words, and staring dully and intently at the priest.
“Why not?” asked the priest, with good-humored surprise.
Grigory said nothing for some time. “It’s a confusion of nature,” he muttered, vaguely but firmly, obviously unwilling to say more.

They laughed and, of course, christened the poor baby. Grigory prayed earnestly at the font, but his opinion of the newborn child stayed the same. Still, he didn’t interfere in any way. As long as the sickly infant lived, he hardly looked at it. He tried, in fact, not to notice it, and for the most part kept out of the cottage. But when, after a fortnight, the baby died of thrush, he laid the child in its little coffin himself and looked at it in deep grief. When they were filling in the shallow little grave, he fell on his knees and bowed down to the earth. For years afterwards he never mentioned his child, and Marfa never spoke of the baby in front of him. Even when Grigory wasn’t there, she never spoke of it above a whisper. Marfa noticed that from the day of the burial he devoted himself to “religion.” He took to reading the _Lives of the Saints_, mostly sitting alone and in silence, and always putting on his big, round, silver-rimmed spectacles. He rarely read aloud, perhaps only in Lent. He was fond of the Book of Job. He had somehow got hold of a copy of the sayings and sermons of “the God-fearing Father Isaac the Syrian,” and he read it persistently for years on end. He understood very little of it, but perhaps prized and loved it all the more for that. Lately he had begun to listen to the teachings of the sect of Flagellants living in the neighborhood. He was plainly shaken by them, but judged it improper to go over to the new faith. His habit of theological reading gave him an expression of still greater gravity.

He was perhaps inclined to mysticism. And the birth of his deformed child, and its death, had been accompanied, as if by special design, by another strange and marvelous event, which, as he said later, left a “stamp” upon his soul. On the very night after the burial of his child, Marfa was woken by the wail of a newborn baby. She was frightened and woke her husband. He listened and said he thought it sounded more like someone groaning, “it might be a woman.” He got up and dressed. It was a rather warm night in May. As he went down the steps, he distinctly heard groans coming from the garden. But the gate from the yard into the garden was locked at night, and there was no other way in, because the garden was enclosed all round by a strong, high fence. Grigory went back into the house, lit a lantern and took the garden key. His wife was in hysterics, still convinced that she heard a child crying, and that it was her own baby crying and calling for her. He paid no attention to her and went into the garden in silence. There he heard at once that the groans came from the bath-house standing near the garden gate, and that they were the groans of a woman. He opened the door of the bath-house and saw a sight that turned him to stone. An idiot girl who wandered about the streets, known to the whole town by the nickname of Lizaveta Smerdyastchaya (Stinking Lizaveta), had got into the bath-house and had just given birth to a child. She lay dying with the baby beside her. She said nothing, for she had never been able to speak. But her story needs a chapter to itself.
